title: Infectious Vascular Diseases
subject: Cardiovascular System (CARD)
author: Dr. Sharilyn Rennie

overview.intro: This chapter covers infections whose main damage falls on the heart or blood vessels: bacterial endocarditis, Chagas disease, Lyme disease, Rocky Mountain spotted fever, the viral hemorrhagic fevers, and viral myocarditis. Each one is traced from the organism and its route of entry to the cell or tissue it injures, and from there to the findings a board question gives you. Three patterns recur: a damaged surface on which organisms settle (endocarditis), an organism that lives in heart muscle or conduction tissue (Chagas, Lyme, myocarditis), and an organism or immune response that injures endothelium and clotting (spotted fever and hemorrhagic fevers). If you can name the vector, the target cell, and the mechanism of injury, you can predict the presentation.
prerequisites: Valve anatomy, pressure gradients, and normal flow through the heart (CV-3, CV-4)
Endothelial control of permeability and coagulation, including tissue factor and platelet adhesion
Type III (immune complex) hypersensitivity and complement
Structure and classification of bacteria, protozoa, and RNA viruses (CV-17)
Conduction system anatomy and AV block on the ECG (CV-7)

connections.how: Rheumatic, degenerative, and congenital valve lesions create the turbulent jets and damaged endothelium on which subacute endocarditis develops.
Chagas disease and viral myocarditis are infectious causes of dilated cardiomyopathy.
Lyme carditis, Chagas disease, and a perivalvular abscess from endocarditis all present with AV block because they inflame or destroy conduction tissue.
Circulating immune complexes in endocarditis deposit in glomeruli and cause a hypocomplementemic proliferative glomerulonephritis.
Endothelial injury in spotted fever and hemorrhagic fevers consumes platelets and clotting factors, the same process that underlies disseminated intravascular coagulation.

terms.def: A mass of platelets, fibrin, inflammatory cells, and organisms attached to a valve or endocardial surface.
Sterile platelet and fibrin deposits on a valve that can later be colonized by circulating bacteria.
Brief entry of bacteria into the blood, for example from the gums or the gut, that is normally cleared within minutes.
Extension of valve infection into the annulus and surrounding myocardium.
An aneurysm caused by infection of an arterial wall, usually from septic emboli lodging in the vasa vasorum or lumen; the name does not mean a fungal cause.
The intracellular, nonflagellated replicating form of Trypanosoma cruzi found in muscle and other tissue cells.
The expanding red skin lesion at the site of an Ixodes tick bite that marks early localized Lyme disease.
Inflammation and injury of the vessel wall; in rickettsial disease it results from infection of endothelial cells.
An eosinophilic, shrunken apoptotic hepatocyte, classically seen in yellow fever.
Increased viral entry into Fc receptor bearing cells when non-neutralizing antibodies from a previous infection coat the virus.
Loss of fluid and protein from capillaries through damaged or activated endothelium, causing hemoconcentration, effusions, and shock.
A junctional protein on cardiac myocytes that coxsackie B viruses and adenoviruses use to enter heart muscle.

sections.title: How vegetations form and which organism to expect

blocks.text: Infective endocarditis is infection of the endocardium, almost always on a valve. Normal endothelium resists bacterial attachment, so most cases need two conditions at once: a surface that bacteria can grip and bacteria in the blood. The surface is created by turbulent, high-velocity flow. A regurgitant or stenotic jet, a ventricular septal defect, a prosthetic ring, or repeated injection of particulate material injures the endothelium and exposes subendothelial collagen and tissue factor. Platelets and fibrin deposit on the injured area, forming a small sterile mass called nonbacterial thrombotic endocarditis.

Bacteria entering the blood during a transient bacteremia bind this deposit. Viridans streptococci produce extracellular dextran (a glucan) and other adhesins that stick to fibrin and platelets, so they need a damaged valve. Staphylococcus aureus carries surface proteins that bind fibrinogen and fibronectin and can attach to and invade intact endothelium, so it infects normal valves and produces acute disease. Neutrophils penetrate this avascular mass poorly, so bacteria grow to very high densities and shed continuously into the blood, which is why bacteremia is persistent rather than intermittent.

Vegetations usually sit along the line of valve closure, on the atrial surface of the mitral and tricuspid valves and the ventricular surface of the aortic and pulmonary valves, the low-pressure sides that receive a regurgitant jet. Left-sided valves (mitral, then aortic) are involved most often because they work at higher pressures. Injection drug use is the main exception: injected bacteria and particulate debris reach the right heart first, and the tricuspid valve is the most common site.

blocks.title: Formation of a vegetation
steps: Turbulent jet or foreign material injures valve endothelium
Collagen and tissue factor exposed; platelets and fibrin deposit
Sterile deposit forms (nonbacterial thrombotic endocarditis)
Transient bacteremia: organisms adhere through dextran or binding proteins
More fibrin covers bacteria and shields them from neutrophils
Vegetation grows and sheds organisms into the blood continuously
blocks.caption: Staphylococcus aureus can skip the first three steps and infect a normal valve.

blocks.text: The organism follows from the source of the bacteremia and the surface available. Acute endocarditis from a virulent organism destroys a valve over days; subacute disease from a low-virulence organism smolders for weeks with fever, weight loss, and fatigue.

blocks.title: Predicting the organism by setting
rows: Native valve, acute course, often a normal valve
Most common cause overall; adhesins allow invasion of intact endothelium
Native damaged valve after dental work
Viridans streptococci (for example S. sanguinis, S. mutans)
Mouth flora enter blood from gums; dextran binds fibrin and platelets
Skin flora injected; tricuspid valve most often affected
Staphylococcus epidermidis and other coagulase-negative staphylococci
Biofilm on foreign material; skin flora introduced at operation
GI or GU procedures, older adults
Gut and urinary flora enter blood during manipulation
Associated with colorectal cancer, so the colon is examined

blocks.caption: Late prosthetic valve infection behaves more like native valve disease, with streptococci and S. aureus becoming common.

blocks.title: Reasoning from setting to organism
blocks.text: A 64-year-old with known mitral regurgitation has had low-grade fever and weight loss for 6 weeks after a tooth extraction. The slow course means a low-virulence organism, the regurgitant valve supplies the deposit, and the extraction released mouth flora: a viridans streptococcus. Now a 28-year-old who injects drugs has 4 days of high fever, a new holosystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border, and nodular lung lesions. The short course means a virulent organism, the murmur is tricuspid regurgitation, and the lung lesions are septic emboli from the right heart: Staphylococcus aureus.

Every complication of endocarditis comes from one of four processes: local destruction of the valve and surrounding tissue, fragments breaking off the vegetation (embolism), immune complexes formed against the persistent bacteremia, and infection of arterial walls. Sorting findings by these processes is easier than memorizing a list.
Local destruction

Bacterial enzymes and neutrophil products perforate leaflets, tear chordae, and erode the valve, causing new or worsening regurgitation. Sudden severe regurgitation gives the ventricle no time to dilate, so acute heart failure with pulmonary edema follows; heart failure is the leading cause of death in endocarditis. Infection can also spread into the annulus as a perivalvular (ring) abscess. This is most common with the aortic valve and with prosthetic valves. Because the aortic annulus lies next to the AV node and His bundle, a new and lengthening PR interval or higher degree AV block in a patient with endocarditis suggests an abscess. Abscesses can also form fistulas between chambers.
Embolism and the side of the heart

Fragments travel downstream from the infected valve. From the left heart they enter the systemic circulation and cause stroke or brain abscess, infarcts or abscesses of the spleen and kidney, and ischemic limbs or digits. Janeway lesions, painless hemorrhagic macules on the palms and soles, are usually attributed to septic microemboli. From the right heart, fragments lodge in the lungs as septic pulmonary emboli, seen as multiple peripheral nodules that may cavitate, with cough, pleuritic pain, and hemoptysis. Large, mobile vegetations embolize most often.
Immune complexes and arterial infection

Continuous antigen release drives antibody production, and antigen and antibody combine into circulating immune complexes (type III hypersensitivity). Deposited in glomeruli, they activate complement and cause a proliferative glomerulonephritis with hematuria, red cell casts, and low complement levels. Osler nodes (painful nodules on finger and toe pads) and Roth spots (retinal hemorrhages with pale centers) are classically attributed to immune complex vasculitis, and rheumatoid factor may be positive. A mycotic aneurysm forms when septic emboli lodge in the vasa vasorum or lumen of an artery and weaken its wall; cerebral arteries, especially branches of the middle cerebral artery, are typical, and rupture causes intracranial hemorrhage.

blocks.title: Complications sorted by mechanism
rows: Acute regurgitation, heart failure, chordal rupture
Aortic or prosthetic valve, new PR prolongation
Stroke, splenic and renal infarcts, Janeway lesions, splinter hemorrhages
Neurologic deficit, flank or left upper quadrant pain
Hematuria with red cell casts, low complement
Sudden headache or hemorrhage weeks into illness
blocks.caption: Splinter hemorrhages under the nails are linear and nonspecific; they also follow trauma.

blocks.predict: Two patients have endocarditis with emboli. One has a splenic infarct and a stroke; the other has multiple cavitating lung nodules. Which valve is infected in each?
blocks.explain: Emboli lodge in the first capillary bed downstream. Systemic infarcts mean a left-sided valve (mitral or aortic). Lung lesions mean a right-sided valve, usually the tricuspid in injection drug use.

blocks.text: Chagas disease is infection with Trypanosoma cruzi, a flagellated protozoan found in Mexico, Central America, and South America. Its vectors are triatomine (reduviid, or kissing) bugs, which live in cracks in mud and thatch houses and feed at night, often on the face. The bug defecates while or after feeding, and infective trypomastigotes in the feces are rubbed into the bite wound or onto the conjunctiva or other mucosa. The parasite is also spread by blood transfusion, organ transplantation, from mother to fetus, and by food or drink contaminated with bug feces. In nonendemic countries, most cases are in immigrants from endemic regions.

At the entry site trypomastigotes invade local cells, transform into intracellular amastigotes, multiply, and burst out as trypomastigotes that spread through the blood. The acute phase lasts weeks to about two months, and most infections are mild or unnoticed. Local inflammation produces a chagoma (an indurated skin lesion) at a skin entry site or Romana sign, painless unilateral swelling of the eyelids, when entry is through the conjunctiva. Trypomastigotes are numerous enough in the acute phase to be seen on a blood smear. A small minority, mainly young children and immunocompromised people, develop acute myocarditis or meningoencephalitis.

The immune response controls but does not clear the parasite, and most people enter a lifelong indeterminate phase without symptoms. Years to decades later, about 20 to 30 percent develop chronic disease. Parasites persist in cardiac muscle and enteric neurons, and the continuing inflammation, with an autoimmune contribution, causes patchy myocardial fibrosis, destruction of conduction tissue, and loss of myenteric (Auerbach) plexus neurons. Tissue sections show lymphocytic infiltrates and fibrosis with few parasites. Parasitemia is now too low for a smear, so chronic disease is identified by antibodies against T. cruzi.

blocks.title: Acute versus chronic Chagas disease
rows: Years to decades later, in about 20 to 30 percent
Few; persist in heart and gut tissue
Fever, chagoma, Romana sign, lymphadenopathy; often no symptoms
Fibrosis, conduction block, apical aneurysm, thrombi, arrhythmia
blocks.caption: Most infected people never progress beyond the indeterminate phase.

blocks.title: From bug bite to chronic organ damage
steps: Triatomine bug feeds and defecates near the bite or eye
Trypomastigotes enter wound or conjunctiva (chagoma, Romana sign)
Amastigotes multiply in cells; parasites spread through blood
Immune control without clearance: indeterminate phase
Years of inflammation: myocardial fibrosis and myenteric neuron loss
Cardiomyopathy with block; megaesophagus and megacolon
blocks.caption: Chronic Chagas disease reflects decades of low-grade parasite persistence and inflammation.

blocks.text: Chronic Chagas cardiomyopathy is a dilated cardiomyopathy with three distinctive features. Fibrosis of the conduction system produces right bundle branch block, often with left anterior fascicular block, and AV block. Thinning of the left ventricular apex produces an apical aneurysm in which mural thrombus forms and embolizes. Scarred myocardium supports reentrant ventricular tachycardia, so sudden death may be the first sign. In the gut, loss of myenteric neurons abolishes coordinated peristalsis and sphincter relaxation, giving an achalasia-like megaesophagus with dysphagia and megacolon with severe constipation.

Lyme disease is caused by Borrelia burgdorferi, a spirochete transmitted by Ixodes ticks (Ixodes scapularis, the black-legged or deer tick, in the eastern United States). Risk is concentrated in the Northeast, the mid-Atlantic states, and the upper Midwest (Wisconsin and Minnesota), where these ticks are common, with a smaller focus on the Pacific coast carried by Ixodes pacificus. White-footed mice are the main reservoir, and deer sustain the adult tick population. Most infections are acquired in late spring and summer from nymphs, which are tiny and easily missed. The spirochete sits in the tick midgut and must migrate to the salivary glands after feeding begins, so transmission usually requires attachment for more than about 36 hours.

The stages follow the spirochete as it spreads. It first moves outward through the skin from the bite, and the inflammatory response at its advancing edge produces erythema migrans, an expanding red patch at least about 5 cm across that may clear centrally into a target shape. It then disseminates through the blood to other skin sites, nerves, meninges, heart, and joints. Late disease reflects persistent organisms or antigen in tissue and the immune response against them. The same tick can transmit Babesia and Anaplasma, so coinfection is possible.

blocks.title: Stages of Lyme disease
rows: Early localized: days to about 1 month
Erythema migrans; fever, fatigue, headache, myalgia
Spirochete spreading through skin around the bite
Multiple erythema migrans lesions; facial nerve palsy (unilateral or bilateral); lymphocytic meningitis; radiculoneuritis; carditis with AV block
Bloodstream spread to skin, nerves, meninges, and heart
Recurrent arthritis of large joints, especially the knee; chronic neuropathy or encephalopathy
Persistent antigen and immune inflammation in synovium and nerve
blocks.caption: Not every patient passes through every stage, and many do not recall the tick bite.

blocks.text: Lyme carditis occurs in a small percentage of untreated patients during early dissemination. Spirochetes and a lymphocytic infiltrate inflame the myocardium and the conduction system, most often at the AV node. The result is AV block of any degree, from a prolonged PR interval to complete heart block, and the degree can change within hours. Because the node is inflamed rather than scarred, the block usually resolves. Myopericarditis can occur but heart failure is uncommon. A young person from an endemic area with a summer rash, facial palsy, or new heart block should raise the diagnosis.

Diagnosis rests on the biology of the antibody response. Erythema migrans appears before antibodies are reliably detectable, so early localized disease is recognized clinically in an exposed patient. Disseminated and late disease are confirmed by serology, usually a screening immunoassay followed by a confirmatory test such as an immunoblot. Bilateral facial palsy is unusual and helps point to Lyme disease rather than idiopathic (Bell) palsy.

sections.title: Rocky Mountain spotted fever as rickettsial vasculitis

blocks.text: Rocky Mountain spotted fever is caused by Rickettsia rickettsii, a small obligate intracellular gram-negative bacterium that stains poorly with Gram stain. It is carried by Dermacentor ticks (the American dog tick in the east and the Rocky Mountain wood tick in the west), and in parts of Arizona and Mexico by the brown dog tick. Despite the name, most United States cases occur in the southeastern and south-central states, such as North Carolina, Tennessee, Arkansas, Missouri, and Oklahoma, in spring and summer. Symptoms begin about 2 to 14 days after the bite.

The target cell explains the disease. Rickettsiae attach to vascular endothelial cells through outer membrane proteins, are taken up, and escape the phagosome into the cytoplasm. There they multiply and polymerize host actin into tails that push them into neighboring endothelial cells, so infection spreads cell to cell along the vessel. Infected endothelial cells and the inflammatory response to them produce a disseminated small vessel vasculitis in skin, brain, lungs, kidneys, heart, and gut.

blocks.title: From tick bite to multiorgan failure
steps: Dermacentor tick transmits Rickettsia rickettsii
Rickettsiae infect endothelium and spread cell to cell by actin
Small vessel vasculitis throughout the body
Increased permeability: edema, hypovolemia, low albumin and sodium
Red cells escape: petechial rash; platelets consumed
Severe cases: shock, pulmonary edema, encephalitis, renal failure
blocks.caption: Each finding is a consequence of injured, leaky endothelium.

blocks.text: The classic triad is fever, headache, and rash with a history of a tick bite or exposure, but all three are present at first in only a minority, and some patients never develop a rash. The rash usually appears on about day 2 to 5 as small blanching pink macules on the wrists and ankles. It spreads centripetally to the arms, legs, and trunk and becomes petechial as red cells leak from damaged capillaries. Involvement of the palms and soles is characteristic but often late. Myalgia, nausea, vomiting, and abdominal pain are common and can mislead toward a gastrointestinal illness.

Laboratory findings follow the vascular injury. Platelets adhere to damaged endothelium and are consumed, causing thrombocytopenia. Fluid and albumin leak into tissues, causing edema and hypoalbuminemia, and the fall in effective circulating volume stimulates ADH release, causing hyponatremia. Liver enzymes may rise. In severe disease, leakage in the lungs causes noncardiogenic pulmonary edema, brain involvement causes confusion, seizures, or coma, and hypovolemia with myocardial involvement causes shock and acute kidney injury. Disseminated intravascular coagulation and gangrene of digits can occur but are less common. Because the course can be rapidly fatal, the diagnosis is made on clinical grounds; antibodies are often absent in the first week.

blocks.title: Rashes that involve the palms and soles
rows: Starts at wrists and ankles, spreads to trunk; fever, headache, tick exposure
Copper-colored macules or papules; generalized lymphadenopathy; condylomata lata
Hand, foot, and mouth disease (coxsackie A)
Vesicles on hands and feet with oral ulcers, usually in young children
Janeway lesions on palms and soles with fever and a murmur
blocks.caption: Palm and sole involvement narrows the differential but does not identify the cause on its own.

blocks.predict: Why does a patient with Rocky Mountain spotted fever develop both edema and a low platelet count, when neither the liver nor the marrow is the primary target?
blocks.explain: Both come from endothelial injury. Damaged, leaky capillaries let plasma and albumin escape into tissues, and exposed subendothelium consumes platelets as they adhere. The marrow is producing platelets; they are being used up at the vessel wall.

blocks.text: Yellow fever and dengue are both flaviviruses (enveloped, positive-sense single-stranded RNA viruses) carried mainly by Aedes aegypti, a daytime-biting mosquito that breeds in standing water near houses. They differ in the organ they damage. Yellow fever is above all a hepatitis with bleeding, while dengue is a febrile illness whose dangerous form is a capillary leak.
Yellow fever

Yellow fever occurs in tropical Africa and South America. A jungle (sylvatic) cycle between monkeys and forest mosquitoes maintains the virus, and Aedes aegypti carries it between people in towns. After 3 to 6 days the illness begins with fever, headache, myalgia, and back pain, and most patients recover. About 15 percent improve briefly and then enter a toxic phase. The virus damages hepatocytes, especially in the middle of the lobule (zone 2, midzonal necrosis), which is unusual because most toxic and ischemic injury is centrilobular. Dying hepatocytes undergo apoptosis and appear as Councilman bodies, shrunken eosinophilic cells, with microvesicular fat and relatively little inflammation. Liver failure causes jaundice, which gives the disease its name, and the loss of clotting factor synthesis combines with platelet consumption to cause bleeding. Blood swallowed or vomited after gastric bleeding is darkened by acid, producing black vomit. Kidney failure and shock follow, and a large share of patients in the toxic phase die.
Dengue

Dengue is widespread throughout the tropics and subtropics and has four serotypes (DENV-1 to DENV-4). Classic dengue causes sudden high fever, often 39 to 40 °C (102.2 to 104 °F), headache with pain behind the eyes, rash, and severe muscle, joint, and bone pain (breakbone fever), with leukopenia and thrombocytopenia. Severe dengue usually appears around defervescence, about days 3 to 7, when endothelial activation by viral proteins and cytokines makes capillaries leak plasma. Hematocrit rises as plasma is lost, pleural effusions and ascites form, and hypovolemic shock can follow, while platelets fall and bleeding may occur. Severe dengue is more likely in a second infection with a different serotype because of antibody-dependent enhancement, and in infants who carry maternal antibody.

blocks.title: Yellow fever versus dengue
rows: Monocytes, macrophages, dendritic cells; endothelium affected
Jaundice, black vomit, bleeding, renal failure
Severe myalgia and arthralgia, retro-orbital pain, rash
Very high aminotransferases, bilirubin, long prothrombin time
Low platelets, low white cells, rising hematocrit
Second infection with a different serotype
blocks.caption: Both are Aedes-borne flaviviruses with thrombocytopenia and bleeding; the liver separates them.

blocks.title: Why the second dengue infection is worse
blocks.text: A traveler had dengue serotype 1 three years ago and now acquires serotype 2. Her antibodies to serotype 1 bind serotype 2 but do not neutralize it. The Fc portion of the bound antibody attaches to Fc gamma receptors on monocytes and macrophages, so more virus enters these cells than would enter without antibody. Viral load and cytokine release rise, and on day 5, as her fever falls, her hematocrit climbs from 40% to 48% while platelets drop to 30,000/microliter. The rising hematocrit is the sign of plasma leaving the vessels, and it warns of shock before blood pressure falls.

sections.title: Shared mechanism of viral hemorrhagic fevers; Ebola and Marburg

blocks.text: Viral hemorrhagic fever is a syndrome rather than one disease. It is caused by enveloped RNA viruses from several families, including flaviviruses (yellow fever, dengue), filoviruses (Ebola, Marburg), arenaviruses (Lassa), and bunyaviruses (hantaviruses, Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever). Despite the name, visible bleeding is often modest; the deaths come mainly from loss of fluid out of the vessels, shock, and multiorgan failure. The viruses share three effects that produce this picture.

First, they infect monocytes, macrophages, and dendritic cells early and spread with them to lymph nodes, liver, and spleen. Many of these viruses block type I interferon signaling, so replication outpaces the innate response, and infected dendritic cells fail to start an effective adaptive response while many lymphocytes die by bystander apoptosis. Second, infected macrophages release large amounts of TNF-alpha, IL-1, IL-6, and other mediators (a cytokine storm), and these, together with direct infection of endothelium in some viruses, loosen endothelial junctions and increase permeability. Third, activated macrophages express tissue factor, which starts coagulation throughout the circulation. Platelets and clotting factors are consumed faster than they are made, which is consumptive coagulopathy (disseminated intravascular coagulation), and hepatocyte injury lowers clotting factor production further. The patient therefore leaks plasma and bleeds at the same time.

blocks.title: Common pathway of hemorrhagic fever viruses
steps: Virus infects macrophages, dendritic cells, and in some cases endothelium
Interferon blocked; replication spreads to liver, spleen, lymph nodes
Cytokine storm: TNF-alpha, IL-1, IL-6 released
Endothelial junctions loosen: plasma leak, hypovolemia
Macrophage tissue factor triggers consumptive coagulopathy
Low platelets and factors, liver injury: bleeding
Shock and multiorgan failure
blocks.caption: Plasma leak and coagulopathy develop together, so shock and bleeding coexist.

blocks.text: Filoviruses: Ebola and Marburg

Ebola and Marburg viruses are filoviruses, enveloped, nonsegmented, negative-sense single-stranded RNA viruses with long filamentous virions. Fruit bats are the likely reservoir, and outbreaks begin when a person handles an infected animal or its tissues, or enters bat-inhabited caves or mines in the case of Marburg. They occur in sub-Saharan Africa. Spread between people is by direct contact with the blood, vomit, stool, or other body fluids of a symptomatic patient or a body after death, or with contaminated objects. Health care workers and people preparing bodies for burial are therefore at high risk, while ordinary airborne spread does not occur. Patients become infectious when symptoms start, viral load rises as illness worsens, and virus can persist in semen and other protected sites for months after recovery.

After an incubation of about 2 to 21 days, illness starts with sudden fever, weakness, myalgia, and headache, followed by profuse vomiting and diarrhea that cause severe fluid and electrolyte loss. A maculopapular rash, conjunctival injection, and bleeding from gums, venipuncture sites, or the gut may appear in the second week. Laboratory findings include thrombocytopenia, leukopenia, high aminotransferases, and evidence of coagulopathy and kidney injury. Case fatality is high: about 50 percent on average for Ebola, ranging widely between outbreaks, and similarly high for Marburg.

blocks.title: Viruses that cause hemorrhagic fever
blocks.caption: All are enveloped RNA viruses; only the first two rows are named in this competency.

blocks.text: Myocarditis is inflammation of the myocardium with injury to myocytes that is not caused by ischemia. Viruses are the most common cause in developed countries. Coxsackie B virus, an enterovirus (a nonenveloped positive-sense RNA picornavirus spread by the fecal-oral and respiratory routes), is the classic cause, and adenovirus, parvovirus B19, human herpesvirus 6, influenza, and SARS-CoV-2 are also important. The typical patient is a young adult, more often male, who develops cardiac symptoms one to a few weeks after a respiratory or gastrointestinal illness, because the virus first replicates in the pharynx or gut and then reaches the heart through the blood.

Coxsackie B and adenovirus enter myocytes through the coxsackie-adenovirus receptor (CAR), a junctional protein, and replicate inside them. Injury occurs in overlapping phases. In the first days, viral replication directly damages myocytes. Over the following weeks, the immune response dominates: CD8 cytotoxic T cells and natural killer cells destroy infected myocytes, and cytokines depress contractility. In some patients, inflammation persists or autoimmunity develops against cardiac proteins such as myosin, and progressive myocyte loss with fibrosis leaves a dilated cardiomyopathy. Parvovirus B19 differs in infecting coronary microvascular endothelium rather than myocytes.

blocks.title: Course of viral myocarditis
steps: Viral infection of pharynx or gut
Viremia; coxsackie B enters myocytes through CAR
Direct viral injury to myocytes
T-cell attack: lymphocytic infiltrate with myocyte necrosis
Most recover; some develop persistent inflammation
Fibrosis and dilation: dilated cardiomyopathy
blocks.caption: Most patients recover fully; the minority with persistent inflammation are at risk of chronic dilated cardiomyopathy.

blocks.text: Each finding traces to myocyte necrosis or inflammation. Necrotic myocytes release troponin. Inflamed tissue disturbs conduction and repolarization, so the ECG shows ST and T changes, AV or bundle branch block, or ventricular arrhythmias, and myocarditis is an important cause of sudden death in young athletes. When the pericardium is involved (myopericarditis), chest pain is pleuritic and the ECG may show diffuse ST elevation. Loss of contracting myocytes lowers ejection fraction and causes heart failure with dyspnea, fatigue, and edema. Because chest pain, ST elevation, and raised troponin can mimic infarction, the clue is a young patient with a recent viral illness and normal coronary arteries.

Endomyocardial biopsy shows an inflammatory infiltrate, mainly lymphocytes, with necrosis of adjacent myocytes in a pattern that is not ischemic. Because inflammation is patchy, a single biopsy can miss it. Cardiac MRI often shows edema and late gadolinium enhancement in the subepicardial or midwall layers, unlike the subendocardial or transmural pattern of infarction. Other histologic patterns point to different causes: many eosinophils suggest hypersensitivity or eosinophilic myocarditis, and multinucleated giant cells suggest the rapidly progressive giant cell myocarditis.

blocks.predict: A 23-year-old has chest pain, ST elevation, and a troponin rise one week after a febrile diarrheal illness. Coronary angiography is normal. What would a biopsy most likely show, and why is the troponin raised?
blocks.explain: A lymphocytic infiltrate with adjacent myocyte necrosis, from coxsackie B entering myocytes and cytotoxic T cells destroying them. Troponin rises because myocytes are dying, from inflammation rather than ischemia, which is why the coronary arteries are normal.

integration.text: Microbiology and immunology explain where each infection strikes. The vector and route decide who is exposed: triatomine bugs in Latin America, Ixodes ticks in the Northeast and upper Midwest, Dermacentor ticks in the southeastern and south-central states, Aedes mosquitoes in the tropics, and body fluids for filoviruses. The target cell decides the lesion: valve deposits for endocarditis, myocytes and enteric neurons for Trypanosoma cruzi, conduction tissue for Borrelia, endothelium for Rickettsia, hepatocytes for yellow fever, macrophages and endothelium for the hemorrhagic fever viruses, and CAR-bearing myocytes for coxsackie B. In several of these diseases the host response causes as much damage as the organism, through immune complexes in endocarditis, T cells in myocarditis and Chagas disease, antibody-dependent enhancement in dengue, and cytokines in hemorrhagic fevers.

Pathology and physiology connect these infections to the rest of cardiology. Inflamed or scarred conduction tissue causes the AV block of Lyme carditis, Chagas disease, and perivalvular abscess, and myocyte loss leads to the dilated cardiomyopathy of Chagas disease and chronic myocarditis. Endothelial injury links rickettsial vasculitis and hemorrhagic fevers to the general mechanisms of edema and disseminated intravascular coagulation. The limits matter as well: classic signs such as the triad of spotted fever, Romana sign, or Osler nodes are often absent, so a question usually turns on exposure plus the mechanism, not on a single sign.

summary: Endocarditis needs a vegetation site plus bacteremia: viridans streptococci adhere to sterile platelet-fibrin deposits on damaged valves, while Staphylococcus aureus can invade normal valves.

Expected organisms: S. aureus in acute and injection drug use (tricuspid) disease, viridans streptococci after dental work, S. epidermidis on early prosthetic valves, enterococci after GI or GU procedures, S. gallolyticus with colon cancer.

Endocarditis complications follow four mechanisms: valve destruction and ring abscess (AV block), emboli to systemic organs (left) or lungs (right), immune complex glomerulonephritis, and mycotic aneurysm.

Acute Chagas disease is usually mild with Romana sign or chagoma; years later about 20 to 30 percent develop dilated cardiomyopathy with conduction block and apical aneurysm, megaesophagus, and megacolon.

Lyme disease spreads in stages: erythema migrans; then facial palsy, meningitis, and carditis with fluctuating AV block; then large joint arthritis and late neurologic disease, mainly in the Northeast and upper Midwest.

Rocky Mountain spotted fever is endothelial infection and vasculitis: fever, headache, a rash moving from wrists and ankles to trunk with palms and soles, thrombocytopenia, edema, hyponatremia, and possible shock.

Yellow fever is a hepatitis with midzonal necrosis, Councilman bodies, jaundice, and black vomit; dengue causes severe myalgia and arthralgia, thrombocytopenia, and in severe cases plasma leak with rising hematocrit.

Hemorrhagic fever viruses share macrophage and endothelial infection, interferon evasion, cytokine storm, and consumptive coagulopathy; Ebola and Marburg spread by body fluids and kill about half of those infected.
Viral myocarditis follows a viral illness in a young adult; coxsackie B enters myocytes through CAR, and biopsy shows a lymphocytic infiltrate with myocyte necrosis.

Hypersensitivity disorders and immune complex disease

verify: The cutoff between early and late prosthetic valve endocarditis is given as 60 days in some sources and 1 year in others; confirm which NABNE uses.
The mechanisms of Osler nodes, Janeway lesions, and Roth spots (immune complex vasculitis versus septic microemboli) are debated; this chapter gives the conventional teaching.
Streptococcus gallolyticus (formerly S. bovis biotype I) nomenclature: confirm whether NABNE material uses the older name.
The share of people with chronic T. cruzi infection who develop chronic disease is quoted from about 20 to 40 percent; this chapter uses about 20 to 30 percent.
The minimum tick attachment time for Lyme transmission is quoted as about 24 to 48 hours in different sources; this chapter uses more than about 36 hours.
The proportion of yellow fever patients who enter the toxic phase (about 15 percent) and its fatality, and the average Ebola case fatality (about 50 percent, WHO), vary by source and outbreak.

Dengue severity terminology (dengue hemorrhagic fever and dengue shock syndrome versus the 2009 WHO categories with warning signs and severe dengue) differs among texts; confirm which terms NABNE uses.
Confirm whether NABNE Part I expects the eponyms Romana sign, Councilman body, Janeway lesion, Osler node, and Roth spot, and the spelling Romana or Romana with a tilde.
Taxonomy of hemorrhagic fever viruses has changed (the former Bunyaviridae is now the order Bunyavirales with several families); confirm the level of classification expected.

Requested new diagram names for a future revision: vegetation-sites (valve surfaces where vegetations form and downstream embolic targets for left versus right sided disease) and rmsf-rash-spread (centripetal spread from wrists and ankles).
